R236.decision_summary: R236: H2 slice 2 — `sprag bind-key` / `unbind-key` at runtime, and the decision slice 1 deferred is settled by an artefact slice 1 shipped. The question was where the live table lives while a client is running, and the design doc had named two candidates (re-read on a signal, or a wire slot). Both were written before `list-keys` existed, and `list-keys` decides it: slice 1 made it read `config.toml` with NO DAEMON, so a runtime binding living anywhere else would make that verb print a table nobody is using, with no way for a user to see the difference — R235's finding class exactly. Repairing that would mean teaching `list-keys` to ask a running client, which loses the no-daemon property precisely when a user is editing their config, has no single answer with two clients attached, and needs a query path to a client that does not exist. So THE FILE IS THE LIVE TABLE: `bind-key` EDITS `config.toml` (which tmux's does not, because tmux's config is an imperative script a fact cannot be written back into, while sprag's is declarative TOML), and a running client re-reads it. That buys tmux's `source-file` as a side effect — a config edited in an EDITOR reaches an attached client on the next keystroke, with nothing to invoke.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `bind_key` / `unbind_key`, editing the user's file through `toml_edit` rather than serializing a struct back out — the file is hand-maintained, so comments, ordering and unrelated tables have to survive an edit. Written atomically (temp + rename, existing mode carried over): this is the user's own config and there is no second copy. TWO file rules the layering forces — a bind drops any `[[unbind]]` naming the key (else the edit leaves behind exactly the `BoundAndUnbound` contradiction the reader refuses), and an unbind adds `[[unbind]]` ONLY when the DEFAULT keymap binds the key, because otherwise the line suppresses nothing. Entries are matched by the key PARSED, not by its spelling, so `^o` and `C-o` are one key.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `KeymapFile` — the keymap plus the text it was read from, with `refresh()`. Compares the file's TEXT, not a `(mtime, len)` stamp: the stamp is cheaper and has a hole, and `split-window -h` -> `split-window -v` inside one timestamp tick changes neither field. What that hole produces is a rebind that SOMETIMES does not take. A broken save KEEPS the last good table and reports once, because a client owns the screen and falling back to the defaults would take a user's own bindings away over a typo in an editor.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `ConfigError` becomes an enum — `Content(ProjectError)` beside a new `Unwritable`. A project file is only ever read, so `ProjectError` has no shape for a failed write, and borrowing `Unreadable` for one would tell a user whose disk is full to go and check that their file parses. Same rule the type was invented for, one level in: name the right thing.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `sprag bind-key [-T prefix] KEY ACTION…` (the action is the rest of the line JOINED, so tmux's unquoted `bind-key c split-window -h` and a shell-quoted form are one string) and `sprag unbind-key [-T prefix] KEY`. Both need NO daemon, like `list-keys`. `-T root` is refused BY NAME rather than ignored — it is slice 4's, and accepting it would promise arbitration nothing performs. The key and action are parsed IN THE CLI so a command-line typo is reported as an argument, naming no file; `config::bind_key` therefore takes a `KeySpec` and a `BoundAction` and every error it can report is about the file.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: `refreshed()` re-reads the table in the KEY arm and nowhere else — the only consumer is key routing, so a repaint cannot change what a key means. One read of a few hundred bytes per keystroke, against a routing decision and a repaint that both follow it. NO thread, NO timer, NO watch: the loop stays the pure `select` R226 measured.
verification_bullets: THE GATE IS A PTY TEST WHERE THE SHIPPED CLI EDITS THE FILE UNDER THE SHIPPED CLIENT. Every unit test either drives the table directly or drives a `KeymapFile` in-process, and none can say whether the real binary ever looks at the file again after it starts — the seam where 'at runtime' can be entirely absent with everything green. Its middle claim is what makes the last one discriminating: BEFORE the bind, `prefix c` must do nothing AND must not reach the child, so a client that detached on any unbound key cannot pass. REVERT MEASURED: return the loaded table without calling `refresh` (i.e. read the config once at startup, as slice 1 did) and the test fails at the detach — the client swallows `c` forever while `sprag list-keys` prints it bound.

A REVERT-PROOF PASSED WITH ITS GUARD REMOVED, AND FIXING THE TEST IS THE MORE USEFUL RESULT. `edit_keys` validates the file both BEFORE the edit and after, and dropping the pre-check left the test green: the post-edit read-back refuses the same broken file, so two correct filters in series hid the first (R233's finding, recurring). What only the pre-check can catch is an edit that REMOVES the broken thing — retargeting the very key whose action is unusable reads back clean and would be WRITTEN, silently repairing a line the user never named in a file every client is refusing to start against. The test now runs both cases; the revert fails the second and not the first, which is the point.

SEVEN MORE REVERT-PROOFS, ALL MEASURED RED. Re-rendering the edit through the SERIALIZING toml crate (the realistic alternative implementation) loses the user's comments. Dropping the unbind removal in `bind_key` makes the write fail against its own read-back. Comparing key spellings as raw strings leaves TWO `[[bind]]` entries for one key. Always recording an `[[unbind]]` writes a line about a key no table mentions. `refresh` returning `Ok(false)` unconditionally leaves the client routing to a stale table. Setting the defaults on a failed re-read takes the working bindings away (the first attempt at this revert did NOT reach the error path and passed — the guard was proven only after the revert was corrected).

THE CLI WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, BEFORE AND AFTER, which is what R235 said to do. That live read is what exposed the report defect: `bind-key Up detach-client` printed `bind-key: config.toml: "Up" is not a key`, sending a user to fix a file that was fine over a typo they had just made on the command line. Now an argument names no file and a broken file still names `config.toml`, asserted as a pair.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets, the rustdoc gate (which caught a private-item doc link, run the way R235 recorded), workspace 1299 -> 1315 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 17 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 88 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.

ONE UNRELATED FLAKE OBSERVED AND CHARACTERISED RATHER THAN RETRIED AWAY: `sprag-terminal`'s `rapid_extreme_resize_with_wide_char_input_does_not_accumulate` failed once under a full parallel workspace run, at its own harness guard (`the bash prompt never appeared`). 0 failures in 10 isolated runs. Its `settle` has a hard 3-second cap that a loaded machine can exceed; the crate is untouched by this round. Registered, not fixed.
carry_forward_bullets: A DEFERRED DESIGN DECISION CAN BE SETTLED BY SOMETHING THE PREVIOUS SLICE SHIPPED, NOT BY WEIGHING THE OPTIONS IT NAMED. The slice-1 doc left a fork with two candidates, and both were written before `list-keys` existed. The verb that slice then built made one of them impossible: a table `list-keys` cannot print is a table that can silently disagree with the running client. Before re-opening a fork a design left behind, check what has been BUILT since — the constraint that decides it is often an artefact, not an argument.

A CHEAPER STALENESS CHECK BUYS A NONDETERMINISTIC BUG. `(mtime, len)` is the idiomatic way to notice a file changed, and it misses two same-length writes inside one timestamp tick — which in this file is `split-window -h` becoming `split-window -v`. The failure that produces is 'my rebind sometimes does not take', which is blamed on everything except its cause. Comparing the text is exact and costs a few hundred bytes per keystroke. When the cheap check has a hole, price the hole as the bug it produces, not as the bytes it saves.

TWO CORRECT FILTERS IN SERIES HIDE THE FIRST — AGAIN (R233). A validation before the edit and a read-back after it look redundant on every test where the edit leaves the fault in place. They are not: the case that separates them is the edit that REMOVES the fault, where the second filter passes a write that silently repairs a file the user was never told was broken. When two guards seem redundant, look for the input on which the later one succeeds.

A REVERT-PROOF MUST BE CHECKED FOR REACHING THE PATH IT CLAIMS TO BREAK. Two of this round's reverts passed at first: one because a second filter covered it, one because the patch was inserted after an early `?` return and never executed on the error path. A revert that passes is not evidence the guard is unnecessary — it is evidence the revert missed. Read WHERE the patch landed before drawing the conclusion.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. The GUI's `WidgetCore::keybinding` is empty and now has both a keymap and a live re-reader to adopt (slice 3). tmux's `-n` root table needs arbitration against the pane for every keystroke; `-r` repeat needs a timer in a loop that is a pure select. The PREFIX cannot be rebound from the CLI at all, because that is tmux's `set-option -g prefix` and sprag has no options table — H2's OTHER half, and with it `window-size`, remains untouched; the live re-read covers the user who edits `[keys] prefix` by hand, which is the whole of what a slice-2 verb could have offered.
R236.publishable_decision_summary: R236: H2 slice 2 — `sprag bind-key` / `unbind-key` at runtime, and the decision slice 1 deferred is settled by an artefact slice 1 shipped. The question was where the live table lives while a client is running, and the design doc had named two candidates (re-read on a signal, or a wire slot). Both were written before `list-keys` existed, and `list-keys` decides it: slice 1 made it read `config.toml` with NO DAEMON, so a runtime binding living anywhere else would make that verb print a table nobody is using, with no way for a user to see the difference — R235's finding class exactly. Repairing that would mean teaching `list-keys` to ask a running client, which loses the no-daemon property precisely when a user is editing their config, has no single answer with two clients attached, and needs a query path to a client that does not exist. So THE FILE IS THE LIVE TABLE: `bind-key` EDITS `config.toml` (which tmux's does not, because tmux's config is an imperative script a fact cannot be written back into, while sprag's is declarative TOML), and a running client re-reads it. That buys tmux's `source-file` as a side effect — a config edited in an EDITOR reaches an attached client on the next keystroke, with nothing to invoke.

R237.decision_summary: R237: H2 slice 3 — the GUI on the user's own keymap, and the plan pointed at the one seam in the client that eats what you put in it. Both the slice-1 design doc and the debt register said the work was to fill `WidgetCore::keybinding`, which "is empty today". It is empty, and it is empty ON PURPOSE: sprag declares no primary surface, so pinion routes a keybinding event to the no-op `send_to_primary` and DROPS it — documented in `primary_surface`, and asserted by a test whose own words are "an override here would be a latent input-loss bug". An emptiness with a test on it is not unfinished work, and two rounds of notes read it as exactly that. The keymap went into `route_key` instead, where the GUI's keyboard actually is. The second finding came from RUNNING it, which is what R235 said to do: with key routing as the only re-reader of `config.toml`, the palette could show a keymap error the file no longer had — the palette's own field holds the keyboard while it is open, so no keystroke can reach a pane to clear it. Fixing that introduced a THIRD: re-reading on the report path made an unchanged broken file clear its own report, because a client keeping its own copy of "why" has to guess what `Ok(false)` means. The verdict now lives on `KeymapFile`, the only thing that knows whether it looked.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/keymap.rs: `Keymap::route` + `PrefixMode` + `Routed`, the prefix state machine lifted out of `sprag-tui`'s binary and shared. `Routed::next()` is the transition defined ONCE — total, so a client cannot arm the one-key mode by accident and cannot forget to disarm it. `Routed::Prefix` is a variant rather than a returned pair for that reason: the outcome IS the transition. What stays per-frontend is the DECODE (termwiz events vs pinion key names) and PERFORMING an action, which the two have nothing in common about.

crates/sprag-gui/src/keys.rs (NEW): `ClientKeys` — the user's `KeymapFile`, the prefix mode, and the live re-read. Not reactive: nothing in `view` reads it, so a `Signal` would flip the root owner dirty on every prefix keystroke and arm a repaint with nothing to repaint. The re-read fires from the TWO moments the file's answer is used — routing a keystroke and showing the report — and nowhere else. No thread, no timer, no watch.

crates/sprag-gui/src/input.rs: the mode is taken out in `route_key`'s FIRST statement, before anything looks at what the key is or where it is going; five surfaces there consume a keystroke before the pane is even resolved, so one place that ends the mode is one place that can forget to. The table is then consulted AFTER the pane gate (a keystroke a text field owns is not CONTESTED, and arming a mode there would eat the next character of a search needle) and BEFORE every built-in `Ctrl+Shift+*` chord (a table the user wrote outranks one this binary spells).

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `KeymapFile::load_usable` (always a usable table plus the reason — for a client with no screen to fail on), `KeymapFile::at` (the holder stops hard-coding which file it watches), and `unusable()`. The verdict moved ONTO the file because a caller holding its own copy has to decide what an unchanged read means, and "no news" is indistinguishable from "nothing is wrong" once the fact lives elsewhere.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs: the in-process `Host` implements `HostClient::split`, which only the wire client did — ordered pre-flight, spawn, place, the `split` wire action's order and for its reason. A client whose `prefix %` works over a socket and silently does nothing in-process is an asymmetry no test could see past.
verification_bullets: THE GATE IS THE LIVE GUI SMOKE, for the reason slices 1-2 used a PTY test: it runs the SHIPPED binary against a real daemon in a child process whose environment the harness owns, so it is the one place "the GUI reads the user's config.toml" can be claimed at all. `spawn` gained an isolated `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (the smoke had been reading the developer's real config for the palette's global commands — latent, since this machine has none). The MIDDLE claims discriminate and fail in OPPOSITE directions: a bare `%` must divide nothing, so a client that treated every `%` as a command cannot pass; and `C-b` must arm nothing once the file moves the prefix to `C-a`, so a client holding `Keymap::default()` cannot pass. Both reverts measured.

THE DEFECT THIS ROUND TURNS ON WAS FOUND BY READING PAINTED OUTPUT, not by a test. The palette's report line was read back verbatim from `scene/snapshot` and said `config.toml: "kill-server" is not an action` — correct. Then the file was FIXED and it said the same thing, three runs in a row. Two causes, both real: the report path did not re-read the file, and the harness was dismissing the palette with an `invoke("close")` verb that does not exist, dropping the `Rejected` so every later open was refused and the catalog stayed frozen at the first one. The smoke's own `call` doc warns about exactly that.

TEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL MEASURED RED. `Routed::next` answering `AfterPrefix` for a swallowed key leaves the client eating every keystroke after one typo. Checking `is_prefix` before the armed branch makes `prefix prefix` arm twice instead of sending, so the key becomes unreachable by any program. Routing on `Keymap::default()` fails four tests. Dropping the `refresh` (slice 1's behaviour) leaves a rebind unseen forever. Taking the mode inside the pane block lets it survive a keystroke another surface consumed. Moving the keymap below the clipboard chord makes a rebound prefix unreachable. Forgetting the broken text re-reports the same typo on every keystroke. Dropping the split pre-flight forks the user's shell for a target that was never there. Dropping the re-read on the report path shows a fixed file as broken. Clearing the verdict on an unchanged read loses the report on the second look.

A THIRD DRIFT GUARD in the family R235 started: every key name this client's own chords reserve must be one `sprag_input::is_key_name` accepts, or the keymap holds a key no `[[bind]]` line can reach and no `list-keys` output can explain. pinion's key names are pinion's, so the only names sprag can hold itself to are the ones it spells.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets, the rustdoc gate (run by sourcing it, per R235 — and made to FAIL three times on real dead links before its silence was read as a pass), workspace 1315 -> 1332 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 17 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 88 -> 96 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.

`sprag list-keys` was run against a hand-written config and its output read, the check that caught R235's defect: `prefix C-a`, the self-send followed onto `C-a`, `o` gone, `c` added. No contradiction this time.
carry_forward_bullets: A PLAN CLAIM IS A CLAIM, AND "IT IS EMPTY" IS NOT "IT IS UNFINISHED". Two rounds of notes carried `WidgetCore::keybinding` as the seam this slice would fill. It is the one place in the client where a binding is silently DROPPED, and that was already written down beside it and already asserted by a test. Nothing had to be discovered — only read. Before building what a plan names, read the thing it names.

THE SECOND CONSUMER OF A FILE IS A SECOND PLACE THAT HAS TO RE-READ IT. Slice 2's rule — re-read where the answer is USED — was implemented as "re-read in the key arm", which was correct while key routing was the only reader. A surface that SHOWS the file is also a reader, and the one place it could not be refreshed from was the one place it is shown: the palette holds the keyboard while it is open. When a rule is spelled as a location rather than as a condition, the next consumer inherits the location and loses the rule.

A CLIENT THAT KEEPS ITS OWN COPY OF "WHY" HAS TO GUESS WHAT SILENCE MEANS. `refresh()` answering `Ok(false)` means the file has not moved, which is NOT the same as nothing being wrong — and a caller holding the reason separately cannot tell those apart. Moving the verdict onto the file removed the guess and the state at the same time. Look for this wherever a caller mirrors a fact its source already knows.

A CALL WHOSE REJECTION YOU DROP IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ONE THAT WORKED — and it can make a harness bug read as a mechanism defect for three runs. `invoke("close")` on a palette that has no `close` verb answered `Rejected` into a `let _ =`, leaving the surface open, every later open refused, and the same stale line painted forever. The file's own transport doc had already recorded this failure shape for params; the same rule covers verbs.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. tmux's `-n` root table LOOKS free in the GUI (its own chords are root bindings) but needs action names for six surfaces the vocabulary has no word for, plus the arbitration the terminal client has no answer for. `-r` repeat needs a timer in a pure select loop and a discrete-chord repeat rule in the GUI. The prefix still cannot be rebound from the CLI: that is `set-option -g prefix`, and H2's OTHER half — the options table, and with it `window-size` — remains untouched.

The table is then consulted AFTER the pane gate (a keystroke a text field owns is not CONTESTED, and arming a mode there would eat the next character of a search needle) and BEFORE every built-in `Ctrl+Shift+*` chord (a table the user wrote outranks one this binary spells).

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `KeymapFile::load_usable` (always a usable table plus the reason — for a client with no screen to fail on), `KeymapFile::at` (the holder stops hard-coding which file it watches), and `unusable()`. The verdict moved ONTO the file because a caller holding its own copy has to decide what an unchanged read means, and "no news" is indistinguishable from "nothing is wrong" once the fact lives elsewhere.

crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs: the in-process `Host` implements `HostClient::split`, which only the wire client did — ordered pre-flight, spawn, place, the `split` wire action's order and for its reason. A client whose `prefix %` works over a socket and silently does nothing in-process is an asymmetry no test could see past.
publishable_verification_bullets: THE GATE IS THE LIVE GUI SMOKE, for the reason slices 1-2 used a PTY test: it runs the SHIPPED binary against a real daemon in a child process whose environment the harness owns, so it is the one place "the GUI reads the user's config.toml" can be claimed at all. `spawn` gained an isolated `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (the smoke had been reading the developer's real config for the palette's global commands — latent, since this machine has none). The MIDDLE claims discriminate and fail in OPPOSITE directions: a bare `%` must divide nothing, so a client that treated every `%` as a command cannot pass; and `C-b` must arm nothing once the file moves the prefix to `C-a`, so a client holding `Keymap::default()` cannot pass. Both reverts measured.

THE DEFECT THIS ROUND TURNS ON WAS FOUND BY READING PAINTED OUTPUT, not by a test. The palette's report line was read back verbatim from `scene/snapshot` and said `config.toml: "kill-server" is not an action` — correct. Then the file was FIXED and it said the same thing, three runs in a row. Two causes, both real: the report path did not re-read the file, and the harness was dismissing the palette with an `invoke("close")` verb that does not exist, dropping the `Rejected` so every later open was refused and the catalog stayed frozen at the first one. The smoke's own `call` doc warns about exactly that.

TEN REVERT-PROOFS, ALL MEASURED RED. `Routed::next` answering `AfterPrefix` for a swallowed key leaves the client eating every keystroke after one typo. Checking `is_prefix` before the armed branch makes `prefix prefix` arm twice instead of sending, so the key becomes unreachable by any program. Routing on `Keymap::default()` fails four tests. Dropping the `refresh` (slice 1's behaviour) leaves a rebind unseen forever. Taking the mode inside the pane block lets it survive a keystroke another surface consumed. Moving the keymap below the clipboard chord makes a rebound prefix unreachable. Forgetting the broken text re-reports the same typo on every keystroke. Dropping the split pre-flight forks the user's shell for a target that was never there. Dropping the re-read on the report path shows a fixed file as broken. Clearing the verdict on an unchanged read loses the report on the second look.

A THIRD DRIFT GUARD in the family R235 started: every key name this client's own chords reserve must be one `sprag_input::is_key_name` accepts, or the keymap holds a key no `[[bind]]` line can reach and no `list-keys` output can explain. pinion's key names are pinion's, so the only names sprag can hold itself to are the ones it spells.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets, the rustdoc gate (run by sourcing it, per R235 — and made to FAIL three times on real dead links before its silence was read as a pass), workspace 1315 -> 1332 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 17 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 88 -> 96 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.

`sprag list-keys` was run against a hand-written config and its output read, the check that caught R235's defect: `prefix C-a`, the self-send followed onto `C-a`, `o` gone, `c` added. No contradiction this time.
publishable_carry_forward_bullets: A PLAN CLAIM IS A CLAIM, AND "IT IS EMPTY" IS NOT "IT IS UNFINISHED". Two rounds of notes carried `WidgetCore::keybinding` as the seam this slice would fill. It is the one place in the client where a binding is silently DROPPED, and that was already written down beside it and already asserted by a test. Nothing had to be discovered — only read. Before building what a plan names, read the thing it names.

THE SECOND CONSUMER OF A FILE IS A SECOND PLACE THAT HAS TO RE-READ IT. Slice 2's rule — re-read where the answer is USED — was implemented as "re-read in the key arm", which was correct while key routing was the only reader. A surface that SHOWS the file is also a reader, and the one place it could not be refreshed from was the one place it is shown: the palette holds the keyboard while it is open. When a rule is spelled as a location rather than as a condition, the next consumer inherits the location and loses the rule.

A CLIENT THAT KEEPS ITS OWN COPY OF "WHY" HAS TO GUESS WHAT SILENCE MEANS. `refresh()` answering `Ok(false)` means the file has not moved, which is NOT the same as nothing being wrong — and a caller holding the reason separately cannot tell those apart. Moving the verdict onto the file removed the guess and the state at the same time. Look for this wherever a caller mirrors a fact its source already knows.

A CALL WHOSE REJECTION YOU DROP IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ONE THAT WORKED — and it can make a harness bug read as a mechanism defect for three runs. `invoke("close")` on a palette that has no `close` verb answered `Rejected` into a `let _ =`, leaving the surface open, every later open refused, and the same stale line painted forever. The file's own transport doc had already recorded this failure shape for params; the same rule covers verbs.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. tmux's `-n` root table LOOKS free in the GUI (its own chords are root bindings) but needs action names for six surfaces the vocabulary has no word for, plus the arbitration the terminal client has no answer for. `-r` repeat needs a timer in a pure select loop and a discrete-chord repeat rule in the GUI. The prefix still cannot be rebound from the CLI: that is `set-option -g prefix`, and H2's OTHER half — the options table, and with it `window-size` — remains untouched.

R238.decision_summary: R238: H2's other half — the options table — and the register's own sentence about it was wrong twice. It claimed the prefix cannot be rebound from the CLI because that is `set-option -g prefix` and sprag has no options table, and that `window-size` comes with it. Reading the code first (R237's rule) overturned both. sprag HAS options: seven live settings spelled as ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, one named `SPRAG_DETACH_ON_DESTROY`, whose own doc had already written this round's premise down — "a future runtime set-option would write the SAME enum, so the policy, not this env, is the durable seam". So the work was never to invent a mechanism over a greenfield; it was to give an existing, undiscoverable surface a name, a type and a way to enumerate it, and the risk was never an empty table but TWO AUTHORITIES for one setting. And `window-size` is not free with the table: the host tracks no attached-client geometry at all, while `sprag-tui`'s own doc states the de-facto policy ("Latest attach wins the pane's size"), so three of tmux's four values would name a policy nothing performs — a MECHANISM slice, not an option slice.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs (NEW): `OptionSpec` + `OPTIONS` — a REGISTRY rather than a struct with a field per setting, because a struct can hold a setting but cannot ENUMERATE it, and a setting nobody can discover is one nobody can use. It holds no VALUE: `OPTIONS` describes the option space and `Options` is what the file says, so a default is computed nowhere and stored nowhere and there is no second copy to go stale. `OptionKind` carries each option's vocabulary WITH it — a key is whatever `KeySpec` parses (so the option space and the keymap cannot drift), a choice is a fixed list (so a bad value is answered with the alternatives). `OptionSetting::parse` is the ONE canonicalisation site, used by the CLI and the file reader alike, and the only way to name a setting to a writer.

`[keys]` BECOMES `[options]`, absorbing its one member. `prefix` is an option in tmux's taxonomy, and two spellings for one setting is the defect class this front keeps meeting; `[keys]` existed to hold "client-wide key settings that are not a binding" and had exactly one. Free: there is no `config.toml` on this machine and none in the repository, so every occurrence was a fixture or a doc line.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `build` replaces `build_keymap` and returns BOTH tables — one act of validation over one document, so a caller cannot get a keymap out of a file whose options are broken. The ORDER is load-bearing: options first, because the keymap's prefix comes out of them. `KeymapFile` becomes `ClientConfig` and holds both, because a second holder of one file would mean a second staleness verdict and two answers to "what does the file say now".

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `set_option` / `unset_option` reuse slice 2's `edit_config` wholesale (comment-preserving, atomic, validated through the ordinary reader before AND after). An unset that empties `[options]` KEEPS the header — the rule that refuses to rewrite an inline array, one table over: an edit deleting a header nobody asked about has reformatted a file the user maintains.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `show-options [-g]` and `set-option [-g] [-u] NAME [VALUE]`, both needing NO DAEMON. Every option is printed, set or not, because a user who does not know an option's name cannot find it in a file that does not name it. `-g` is accepted (every sprag option is global, so the flag a tmux user's fingers produce must simply work); `-w` / `-p` are refused BY NAME, and `set-window-option` / `show-window-options` are not verbs, because a scope with no members promises an overlay nothing holds.

crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: `SPRAG_DETACH_ON_DESTROY` is RETIRED for the option, and the held copy goes with it — no field, no captured poll-thread parameter, a fresh read at each consultation. The poll thread takes a `Fn() -> DetachOnDestroy` instead of a value, so the reader is INJECTED (the shape `on_change` already had) and the per-policy poll test keeps its power.
verification_bullets: THE GATE IS A PTY TEST WHERE THE SHIPPED CLI SETS AN OPTION UNDER THE SHIPPED CLIENT, for the reason slices 1-3 each needed their own: the unit tests drive an `Options` in process and the CLI tests drive the file with nothing attached, so neither can say whether the client reads `[options]` at all, let alone reads it again after starting. Its three claims fail in DIFFERENT directions: `C-a` reaches the pane before the set (a client that had taken it as a prefix fails), the ABANDONED `C-b d` must reach the pane after it (a client holding a stale table DETACHES here instead — the discriminating claim), and `C-a d` then detaches with no reattach. REVERT MEASURED: drop the `refresh` in `refreshed` and it fails at the second claim, in 16s of timeout.

A REVERT-PROOF PASSED, AND THE REASON WAS THAT I RAN THE WRONG SUITE. Writing the option at the document ROOT instead of inside `[options]` left all 31 config unit tests green — because config.rs had NO unit test for the writer's happy path (the CLI tests carried it). Re-measured against the CLI suite it fails, and the artefact run showed the read-back guard refusing the write with its own explanation. A localised unit test now pins the structure, and ITS revert is measured red.

SIX MORE REVERT-PROOFS, ALL MEASURED RED. Combining the two swaps in `refresh` with `||` short-circuits and leaves the OPTIONS stale on any re-read that moved the keymap — measured, and it reports `Some("on")` beside a new prefix, which is a bug that only appears when an edit touched both. Taking `.take(0)` over the file's options fails four tests. Returning a key value as typed rather than as `KeySpec` spells it fails the canonical test and the cross-verb prefix test. Removing the whole `[options]` table on an unset takes the user's header and comment with it.

THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, before any of it was believed: `show-options` with no file, `set-option prefix ^a` (stored `C-a`), the file after the edit (comment, unrelated table and inline comment intact), `-u`, every error path, `-g`, `-w`, and an inline `options = {...}` (refused with an instruction, while `show-options` still reads it). That read is what confirmed the argument/file split holds in both directions.

THE GUI'S REPORT WAS READ PAINTED, not assumed: a value no option takes now paints `config.toml: detach-on-destroy: "sideways" is not one of: on, off, no-detached, next, previous` in the palette, beside the broken-binding line. A distinct claim from the binding case, since a reader that skipped `[options]` would leave that file looking usable.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets (0), the rustdoc gate run by SOURCING it — which caught two real defects, a public doc linking the private `build` and an `options` link ambiguous between a function and a module — workspace 1332 -> 1354 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 18 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 96 -> 97 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.
carry_forward_bullets: AN OPTION AND AN ENV VAR FOR ONE SETTING ARE TWO AUTHORITIES, AND THE VERB THAT REPORTS IT CANNOT SEE THE ENV. This is why `SPRAG_DETACH_ON_DESTROY` had to be retired rather than kept as an override: `sprag show-options` runs in its own process, so it would print a policy the client it describes is not using — R235's defect class exactly. When a setting gains a first-class home, the old channel is not a fallback, it is a second answer.

NOT EVERY ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE IS AN OPTION WAITING FOR A TABLE. `SPRAG_RESTORE_HISTORY` is named "the OPERATOR's control" and bounds what a pane's output writes to disk; `SPRAG_OSC52` decides whether a program may read the clipboard. `config.toml` is the USER's file and a client re-reads it live, so moving either there would change WHO controls it and make an exposure limit take effect with no daemon restart. Sort a settings surface by WHO it belongs to before migrating it.

A HELD COPY OF A SETTING IS A LIVENESS DECISION IN DISGUISE. The boot-read `detach_on_destroy` field looked like caching; what it actually decided was that `set-option` would not reach a running client. Reading at the moment of use cost nothing (a destroy is rare), deleted a field and a parameter, and made the option as live as the keymap. Where a held value is read on a RARE event, the cache is the bug.

REMOVING AN INJECTED VALUE CAN COST A TEST ITS POWER; INJECT THE READER INSTEAD. Dropping the poll thread's `policy` parameter for a direct config read would have taken the per-policy loop test (whose own doc records that `off` was once missing from a hand-listed guard and silently detached) down with it. A `Fn() -> T` keeps both the freshness and the seam, and it is the shape `on_change` already had.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. `window-size` needs the host to hold attached-client geometry and arbitrate — `latest` is what the code does and the other three values would be settings nothing performs. `history-limit` is TWO things here: a const `SCROLLBACK_CAP` sizing structures on the hot scroll path R218-R221 measured, and a persisted count that is an operator's; an option governing only the second would give a user who set 10000 a thousand live lines. The GUI's own preferences (`gui-font`, `gui-dock-mode`) are the next clean slice.

R239.decision_summary: R239: the options table's second slice — `gui-font` from environment variable to option, a NUMBER kind to hold it, and the singular `show-options -v NAME` read. The finding is that my OWN design doc, written one round earlier and recording R238's lesson, then broke it: its slice-2 list named `gui-dock-mode` because the name appeared in an env-var grep, and that name appears ONLY in a doc comment explaining why the feature was DELETED (as does `SPRAG_GUI_LAYOUT`). A grep cannot tell a live read from an epitaph. Exactly ONE live GUI preference existed, and the slice earns its place by what that one forces: the registry's third value kind, a file value that is not a string, and an honest answer to boot-vs-live. `gui-font` is adopted at a window's BIRTH, and that is a mechanism fact rather than a shortcut — the glyph size decides the measured cell, which decides every pane's grid, so a live change is the resize path plus a wake this client deliberately does not have. Which in turn exposed that a birth-read setting cannot be gated by writing the file under a running window, because such a check passes identically against a client that never read the option: the smoke gained `relaunch_gui`, and the gate is 77 columns against 38.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `OptionKind::Number` — the registry's THIRD value kind, and the first that is not text. A positive integer; zero is refused rather than read as "unset", because an option always HAS a value in force and a caller must never be handed a size of nothing. NO upper bound: a bound nothing measures is taste, and the one candidate (a glyph so large the boot grid is empty) cannot happen because the GUI's `grid_dims` floors at 1x1. Stored as the PARSE renders it, so `007` and ` 7 ` are both `7` — the rule a key already followed.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `GUI_FONT` (`gui-font`), `Options::number`, `OptionSetting::as_number`. The `gui-` prefix is not decoration: it governs ONE frontend and tmux has no twin, so a flat namespace needs the prefix for a user to see which of their clients a setting reaches.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `[options]` values become `toml::Value`, rendered by `declared_value`. `gui-font = 20` is how a person writes a size in a hand-maintained file; demanding `"20"` would be the parser's convenience imposed on the user. Both spellings reach the same validation, so the option's KIND decides what is acceptable rather than the TOML type that was written. Anything else (a float, a bool, a table) is refused while NAMING the option, which serde's own "invalid type" could not do. `set_option` writes a number UNQUOTED for the same reason — a file this CLI edited must not differ from one a human wrote.

crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag.rs: `show-options [-v] [NAME]` — tmux's `show-options -v` and the singular read herdr spells `show-option`, which was the last readable option verb on the parity list. `-v` prints the value ALONE because that is what a script wants: `$(sprag show-options -v prefix)` needs no `cut`, and a value on a line of its own cannot be mis-split by one. `-v` with no name is REFUSED rather than answered with every value — the flag exists to remove an ambiguity, so answering it with a list hands that ambiguity back.

crates/sprag-gui/src/terminal.rs: `font_size_px` reads the option; `SPRAG_GUI_FONT` and the `parse_font_size` it needed are gone. No holder: `crate::keys` owns the one live view of the file, and this is a single read at the moment the value is USED, which for a glyph size is the birth of a window.

crates/sprag-gui/src/bin/sprag-smoke.rs: `Smoke::relaunch_gui` — kill the client, remove the stale socket, spawn a fresh one, reconnect, re-apply the Xvfb OS-focus gate. `gui_log` now reads EVERY client's log rather than the newest, so the run-wide "every painted frame settled" claim does not silently narrow to the last launch.
verification_bullets: THE GATE IS TWO LIVE CLIENT LAUNCHES, because a setting a window adopts at BIRTH cannot be gated the way a keymap is: writing the file under a running window proves nothing when the client is not supposed to notice, so such a check passes identically against a client that never read the option. This is R238's finding recurring inside the very document that recorded it: check that a named thing is READ, not merely mentioned.

A positive integer; zero is refused rather than read as "unset", because an option always HAS a value in force and a caller must never be handed a size of nothing. NO upper bound: a bound nothing measures is taste, and the one candidate (a glyph so large the boot grid is empty) cannot happen because the GUI's `grid_dims` floors at 1x1. Stored as the PARSE renders it, so `007` and ` 7 ` are both `7` — the rule a key already followed.

R240.decision_summary: R240: `default-command` — the first DAEMON-side option, and the boundary my own design doc drew turned out to be narrower than it said. That doc stated "every option here is the CLIENT's" as an invariant and used it, one round later, as the reason `default-command` could not be built. Reading found two things. The statement was a GENERALISATION FROM THREE EXAMPLES (`prefix`, `detach-on-destroy`, `gui-font`), not a fact about the code; and the crossing costs nothing, because the daemon ALREADY reads the user's `config.toml` on every call for the palette's `[[command]]` rows — its own doc says "read from disk on every call". So a daemon-side option adds a READER to a file it was already reading. The invariant that actually holds, and that the module doc now states, is that no option crosses the WIRE: every process that needs one reads the file itself, which is what keeps every option verb answering with no daemon. Four places resolve "no command was specified" and all four now call one resolver, because a setting honoured by some of them is R237's asymmetry. The restore path is deliberately NOT one of them and a test pins it: its fallback to a shell answers "the recorded command is REFUSED", which is a different question with the same shape, and answering it with a user's default would run a program on the strength of a security refusal.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-terminal/src/command.rs: `shell_command_line(line)` — a third assembly form beside `command_from_parts` and `default_shell_command`: `$SHELL -c <line>`, the shape tmux's `default-command` takes. Handed to the shell WHOLE rather than split here, and that is the point — a pipeline, a quoted argument and `sh -c 'exec top'` are the SHELL's grammar, and a splitter of ours would be a second, poorer one. Whether the program exists is the shell's answer too, and it lands in the pane where the user reads it. The LABEL is the command's own first word (a leading `exec ` stripped, a path reduced to its basename, both as tmux's window naming does), because a pane running `htop` that introspects as `bash` is a pane a user cannot find.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: `OptionKind::Command` — the one kind whose vocabulary is genuinely OPEN, and saying so is honest rather than a gap. EMPTY is a valid value meaning "no command", which is why `Number` refusing zero is not the same rule: a size of nothing is not a size, while a command of nothing is a decision. `OptionKind::render` shell-quotes a Command for the `name value` listing, so `default-command ''` says something where a line ending in a space says nothing; `-v` stays RAW because a script asked for the value, not a rendering of it.

crates/sprag-host/src/config.rs: `default_pane_command()` — the ONE resolver for "no command was specified": the user's `default-command`, then `$SHELL`. Four places asked that question (the daemon's spawn/split/new_session/new_window through one spec parser, the in-process host's `new_pane`/`new_window`, the windowed client's boot pane, `sprag-term`'s standalone boot) and a setting honoured by some of them is the asymmetry R237 named. A config that cannot be USED logs and falls through to the shell rather than refusing to birth a pane: the daemon has no screen, and the file's problem is already reported to any client that opens a palette.

crates/sprag-host/src/options.rs: the module's invariant is REWRITTEN. It said "every option here is the CLIENT's"; `default-command` is the counter-example, and the claim was weaker than it looked because the daemon already reads `config.toml` on every call for `[[command]]`. What holds instead — and what keeps every verb daemon-free — is that NO OPTION CROSSES THE WIRE: each process that needs one reads the user's file itself.

crates/sprag-gui/src/terminal.rs, crates/sprag-host/src/bin/sprag-term.rs, crates/sprag-host/src/host.rs, crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the four birth sites now call the resolver. `SPRAG_GUI_CMD` and `sprag-term -- <program>` stay AHEAD of it, because an argv a launcher passed is an explicit choice and `default-command` is by definition what runs when there was none.
verification_bullets: THE GATE IS A REAL DAEMON READING A REAL `config.toml`, and it covers TWO birth paths separately because they are separate code: the standalone boot pane (`sprag-term` with no `--`) and a pane born through the wire `spawn` action (`split-window`, whose spec parser every other daemon-side birth shares). With `default-command = "cat"` both must be labelled `cat`, where a daemon ignoring the option labels them with `$SHELL`'s own name. REVERT MEASURED, and it produced exactly the asymmetry the split-out claims exist to catch: putting `default_shell_command()` back in `parse_spawn` prints `["cat", "/bin/bash"]` — the boot pane honouring the option while a split ignores it, which is R237's "works over a socket, does nothing in process" one layer along.

TWO MORE REVERT-PROOFS, MEASURED RED. Returning `sprag-term`'s boot to `default_shell_command` fails the boot line alone. Labelling a shell command line with the SHELL's label (`command_from_parts`'s own return) fails both the CLI gate and the unit test, with `/bin/bash` where `htop` was asserted — the label is what `sprag panes` prints and what a sidebar shows, so it is the observable half of the feature.

A DELIBERATE EXCLUSION IS PINNED BY A TEST, not by a comment: a RESTORED pane whose recorded program is refused gets a SHELL and never the user's `default-command`. `exact_or_shell`'s fallback answers "the recorded command is REFUSED" — a decision about not re-running what a pane was doing — and that is a different question from "no command was specified". Substituting this option there would run a program on the strength of a security refusal, so a test now says so with a `default-command` set in the config while the assertion reads the shell.

THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, against a live daemon on `default-command = "exec cat"`: the standalone boot pane, a `split-window`, and a `new-window` all reported `cat` through `sprag panes` — three birth paths, one label, and the `exec` prefix stripped as designed. Also read: `show-options` printing `default-command ''` unset and `default-command 'exec top -d 2'` set, `-v` handing back the raw line, and the file itself after an edit.

A TEST CAUGHT A HOLE IN THE LABEL DERIVATION, and the first spelling of that test hid it. `command_line_label` fell back to `unwrap_or(first)` at each step, which answers EMPTY for `exec ` — while its own doc claimed a pane is never labelled with nothing. The test as first written asserted the wrong value for `///` and papered over the empty case with a tautological `assert!(x || !x)`. Both are fixed: every step now declines to what it was given, and the test is written from what the code answers.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets (0), the rustdoc gate (sourced), workspace 1360 -> 1367 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 18 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 101 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs.
carry_forward_bullets: AN INVARIANT I WROTE ONE ROUND EARLIER WAS A GENERALISATION FROM THREE EXAMPLES. "Every option here is the CLIENT's" was true of `prefix`, `detach-on-destroy` and `gui-font`, and it read like a boundary. `default-command` crossed it on the first try, and the crossing cost nothing — the daemon already reads `config.toml` on every call for `[[command]]`, which its own doc says. Before treating a design statement as a constraint, check whether it is a FACT about the code or a summary of the cases built so far; the second kind stops being true without anything breaking.

THE INVARIANT THAT SURVIVED IS THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: no option crosses the WIRE. Each process reads the user's file itself, which is what keeps `show-options` / `set-option` answering with no daemon and what makes "the file IS the live table" hold for a daemon-side setting too. A weaker, truer invariant is better than a memorable false one.

"REFUSED" AND "UNSPECIFIED" ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS WITH THE SAME SHAPE. Both end in "so run a shell", which is exactly why a resolver for one is tempting to reuse for the other. The restore path's shell is a SECURITY decision about not re-running a recorded command; answering it with the user's `default-command` would run a program on the strength of a refusal. When two fallbacks produce the same value, check whether they are answering the same question before merging them.

A VOCABULARY CAN BE LEGITIMATELY OPEN, AND SAYING SO BEATS INVENTING A VALIDATOR. Every other option kind carries a closed vocabulary; a command line's grammar is the user's shell's. A splitter or an existence check here would be a second, poorer shell — and the honest report is the one the shell already gives, IN the pane, where the user is looking.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. `window-size` needs attached-client geometry the host does not hold. `history-limit` is a const on the VT hot path R218-R221 measured plus an operator's persisted count. `default-shell` would be `$SHELL`'s twin and has no consumer distinct from `default-command`'s fallback yet. `WHEEL_ROWS_PER_LINE` is a hardcoded client constant no rival demands.

Before treating a design statement as a constraint, check whether it is a FACT about the code or a summary of the cases built so far; the second kind stops being true without anything breaking.

THE INVARIANT THAT SURVIVED IS THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: no option crosses the WIRE. Each process reads the user's file itself, which is what keeps `show-options` / `set-option` answering with no daemon and what makes "the file IS the live table" hold for a daemon-side setting too. A weaker, truer invariant is better than a memorable false one.

"REFUSED" AND "UNSPECIFIED" ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS WITH THE SAME SHAPE. Both end in "so run a shell", which is exactly why a resolver for one is tempting to reuse for the other. The restore path's shell is a SECURITY decision about not re-running a recorded command; answering it with the user's `default-command` would run a program on the strength of a refusal. When two fallbacks produce the same value, check whether they are answering the same question before merging them.

A VOCABULARY CAN BE LEGITIMATELY OPEN, AND SAYING SO BEATS INVENTING A VALIDATOR. Every other option kind carries a closed vocabulary; a command line's grammar is the user's shell's. A splitter or an existence check here would be a second, poorer shell — and the honest report is the one the shell already gives, IN the pane, where the user is looking.

NOT BUILT, AND EACH REASON IS STILL A MECHANISM. `window-size` needs attached-client geometry the host does not hold. `history-limit` is a const on the VT hot path R218-R221 measured plus an operator's persisted count. `default-shell` would be `$SHELL`'s twin and has no consumer distinct from `default-command`'s fallback yet. `WHEEL_ROWS_PER_LINE` is a hardcoded client constant no rival demands.

R241.decision_summary: R241: `window-size` — the mechanism slice, and the round began by falsifying its own motivating hypothesis. Two clients of different sizes were expected to THRASH, each resizing the panes back to its own screen; measured, they do not, and the reason is the finding: the `resize` action is the one mux action that does not `announce()`, so a resize never bumps the scene and the losing client is never woken. What was actually there was not a race but a SILENT STALE — the pane took the size of whichever client most recently had a layout event, and the other went on painting a grid whose real dimensions it had never been told. So the shape of the work was not "arbitrate a contested write" but "give a pane one authority and tell everyone what it says". That authority is `sprag_terminal::tile`, moved out of `sprag-tui` into the crate that owns `LayoutWire` so both frontends run ONE function, taking the session's arbitrated window rather than the caller's screen. The daemon learns each client's cell area (reported, never measured — it owns no tty), reads `window-size` from the user's file itself, and publishes only the arbitrated `(cols, rows)`. `sprag-gui` is NOT arbitrated and the boundary is stated rather than fudged: its chrome is PER PANE, so the cells it can give the arrangement are not one rectangle minus a constant, and handing it this answer would clip the bottom rows off every pane.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-tui/src/layout.rs -> crates/sprag-terminal/src/tiling.rs: the cell-space tiler MOVES beside `LayoutWire`, and its module doc's claim that the GUI's pixel projection and this one are "deliberately separate" is deleted as the thing that was wrong. Separate projections meant two functions deciding one pane's `(cols, rows)`, which is not a design, it is the defect. `tile` now takes the session's WINDOW; `Rect::intersect` is new, so a client smaller than the window CROPS at paint time while still resizing the pane to its full share — a pane is resized to what the session says and painted to what the terminal has.

crates/sprag-host/src/attach.rs: `ClientSize` + `AttachmentRegistry::size`/`sizes`/`session_of`, and `ClientInfo` gains the area. The struct's own doc said "sprag has no tty/size/activity to report"; that reason SURVIVES and is why the field is a REPORT — the daemon still owns no tty, it is now told. `None` is a real state, so a `smallest` policy is never handed a size nobody has. A `Reported` ordinal orders `latest`, counting attach-or-resize rather than tmux's "most recently USED" — a keystroke carries no client identity, and threading one through the whole input wire to serve one option is not honest cost.

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs (NEW): `WindowSize` + `arbitrate`, folding per DIMENSION rather than picking a client — `largest` over 80x50 and 120x24 is 120x50, which is neither client's own area and is the only rule that keeps the promise the name makes. `latest` is the exception BY CONSTRUCTION, since it names a client and so takes its two numbers together. `None` for no reporter is not "use 80x24": inventing one would reflow every program in the session the moment the last client detached. tmux's `manual` is NOT offered — it needs a stored per-session size and a `resize-window` verb, and a value naming a rule nothing performs is the defect this front keeps finding.

crates/sprag-rpc/src/client.rs + crates/sprag-host/src/rpc.rs: `client/size`, intercepted beside `client/hello` and BEFORE scope resolution because it carries no session — which session it moves is the one that client is attached to, and only the registry knows. Half a size is refused whole: a client that sent one number has a bug this names, not a window whose height came from elsewhere.

crates/sprag-host/src/{options,config,wire,workspace}.rs: the `window-size` option (its vocabulary taken from `WindowSize::name()` so the table and the policy cannot drift, with a test that holds them together), `config::window_size()` reading the user's file per call as `default_pane_command` does, and the `window_size` wire SLOT. The option never crosses the wire; the derived ANSWER does. Default `latest`, because that is what the code already did — a default that changed a solo user's pane sizes would be a behaviour change disguised as a parity feature.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs + crates/sprag-client/src/wire.rs: the TUI reports its area at boot and on every window change and tiles over `window_area(host, screen)`, falling back to its own screen when the host has no window — the honest answer for an older daemon, and exactly what it did before. `sprag list-clients` now prints `[COLSxROWS]`, tmux's own shape, omitted rather than faked for a client that has not reported.
verification_bullets: THE HYPOTHESIS THAT STARTED THE ROUND WAS MEASURED AND FALSIFIED FIRST, before any design. A probe attached two real clients (80x24 and 100x30) to one session and sampled the pane size for 3s: it settled at 100x30 in 263ms and STAYED, through a content bump too. No thrash. Reading found why — `workspace.rs`'s `resize` action, alone among the mux actions, does not `announce()` — and that turned the round from arbitrating a contested write into telling the loser anything at all.

THE GATE IS THREE POLICIES OVER TWO REAL CLIENTS ON REAL PSEUDOTERMINALS AGAINST A REAL DAEMON READING A REAL `config.toml`, with the dimensions CROSSED (100x24 and 80x30, the wider client the shorter one) so the three answers are three DIFFERENT rectangles and neither `largest` (100x30) nor `smallest` (80x24) is any single client's own area — a daemon picking a whole client instead of folding per dimension fails. REVERT MEASURED TWICE: tiling over the client's own screen fails `smallest` and `largest` (not `latest`, which is what the old accident coincided with — the reason `latest` alone could never have gated this); forcing `arbitrate` to always answer `latest` fails the same two.

A REVERT-PROOF PASSED AND THE REASON WAS A STALE BINARY. Forcing `arbitrate` to `latest` left all three green, because the PTY suite spawns a SIBLING `sprag-term` that `cargo test -p sprag-tui` does not rebuild — its assert covers the binary being ABSENT, not being older than the source. Rebuilding the bins first turned the same revert red. Every measurement in this entry was re-taken after `cargo build -p sprag-host --bins`.

A SECOND REVERT-PROOF PASSED, AND THAT ONE STANDS AS A LIMIT RATHER THAN A FIX. Deleting the scene bump from `client/size` leaves the whole gate green INCLUDING the case written to catch it (`a_client_that_reported_nothing_re_tiles_when_the_window_moves`, which asserts the un-reporting client redraws its divider at the narrowed column). The reason is an indirection: the REPORTING client re-tiles and resizes the panes, that reflow marks them dirty, and the dirty path bumps. The announce is kept and its doc now says it is not independently falsifiable and why — that chain is nobody's stated contract, holds only while a window change always resizes a pane, and delivers the wake a reflow late.

THE ARTEFACT WAS RUN AND ITS OUTPUT READ, twice with the input changed. `show-options` lists `window-size latest`; `set-option window-size smallest` writes `window-size = "smallest"` unquoted-key inside `[options]`; `manual` and `""` are refused with `is not one of: largest, smallest, latest`. Then a live daemon with two real clients on controlling terminals: `sprag list-clients` printed `[100x24]` and `[80x30]`, and the pane read `80x30` with no policy set (latest) and `80x24` under `smallest` — the narrowest width and the shortest height, neither client's own area.

Gates green: fmt, clippy --workspace --all-targets (0), the rustdoc gate, workspace 1367 -> 1383 tests passed / 0 failed, the PTY suite 10 consecutive green runs at 22 tests each, live GUI pixel smoke 101 passed / 0 failed on three consecutive runs (unchanged, confirming the GUI was left alone).

THE DOC GATE CAUGHT TWO REAL DEFECTS THAT A SOURCED RUN HAD REPORTED CLEAN, and the first is a rule: `layout` was a PRIVATE module in `sprag-tui`, so its docs were never gated; `pub mod tiling` switches `-D rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links` ON for the same text, which then failed on a link to the private `divide`. The second was a link to `sprag_input::MouseInput` from a crate that does not depend on sprag-input. Making a module public is a doc-gate event.
carry_forward_bullets: A HYPOTHESIS ABOUT A BUG IS STILL A CLAIM, AND MEASURING IT FIRST CHANGED THE WHOLE DESIGN. "Two clients must thrash" was mechanically plausible — each client tiles over its own screen and resizes the panes — and it was wrong, because the resize path wakes nobody. Had the round been designed from it, the work would have been arbitration for a contested write that never happens, and the actual defect (a client painting a grid whose dimensions it was never told) would have survived underneath. Probe the failure before designing the fix, not just the code that would cause it.

AN ACTION THAT DOES NOT ANNOUNCE IS INVISIBLE, AND `resize` IS THE ONE. Every other mux action bumps the scene; `resize` does not, which is why a size can change under a client that never learns. That silence is load-bearing in both directions — it is also why two clients do not fight — so it is a fact to design around rather than a bug to fix blind.

THE PTY SUITE'S DAEMON IS A SIBLING BINARY CARGO DOES NOT REBUILD, AND ITS GUARD ONLY CATCHES ABSENCE. `cargo test -p sprag-tui` builds the tui and the sprag-host LIB, never the `sprag-term` BIN the tests spawn — so a change to the daemon is invisible and a revert-proof passes. `cargo build -p sprag-host --bins` before any measurement through that suite. Existing-but-stale looks exactly like correct.

MAKING A MODULE PUBLIC TURNS THE PRIVATE-INTRA-DOC-LINK GATE ON FOR TEXT THAT ALREADY PASSED. The tiler's module doc was unchanged in the links that failed; it moved from `mod layout` to `pub mod tiling`. This is R224's bin-vs-lib finding one layer along — the gate's scope is a property of the item's VISIBILITY, not of the words.

sprag-gui IS NOT ARBITRATED, AND THE REASON IS A MECHANISM WORTH ITS OWN ROUND. Its chrome is PER PANE (a dock header per panel, plus a sidebar and a tab strip), so the cells it can give the ARRANGEMENT are not its window minus a constant — they depend on the shape of the tiling about to be laid out. Handing it the arbitrated window would size every pane's grid taller than the widget drawn for it and clip the bottom rows. Three encoded contracts also move when it lands: floating panes are their own surfaces and cannot be arbitrated at all, and a live divider drag runs AHEAD of the host tree (the GUI commits a ratio on release, so pane cells would lag a drag). pinion is NOT a blocker — R991.1 already clips an over-large grid to its node rect and pass 0 fills the rect with the terminal background, so both crop and letterbox are already handled upstream.

STILL NOT BUILT: tmux's `window-size manual` and the `resize-window` verb it needs (a per-session stored size, which touches the snapshot/restore surface); `history-limit`, still the VT hot-path const plus an operator's persisted count.

R242.decision_summary: R242: the GUI joins the window, and the derivation moves to the daemon. R241 left sprag-gui out of the arbitration behind a mechanism that is true in every particular — its chrome is PER PANE, so the cells it can give the arrangement are not its window minus a constant — and recorded it as a feature a client misses out on. Probing it first, which is R241's own finding, showed a live defect two commands away: with a window showing two panes at 38x17, attaching a 100x30 terminal to the SAME session made the panes 49x30 while the window went on painting 38x17 of a 49x30 buffer, thirteen rows and eleven columns off screen with nothing to say so. Reading it gave two answers. The GUI need not model its chrome, because pinion already MEASURES each pane's laid-out rect; what it needs is the INVERSE of the tiler, folding those measurements back into one window. And the client-side half could not be finished at all — the window moves when ANOTHER client attaches, resizes or detaches, and sprag-gui has no seam that observes any of those. So the derivation moved to where both of its inputs already live: a pane's size is tile(tree, window), the tree is the daemon's and the window is the daemon's, and a client now writes a pane's size only when the daemon has no window to derive one from.
changes_bullets: crates/sprag-terminal/src/tiling.rs: `fit_window(tree, measured)` — the largest window whose tiling gives every pane no more cells than that pane's surface measured. It is the INVERSE of `tile` and is defined BY it: the search asks `tile` whether a candidate fits rather than doing arithmetic of its own, so there is no second geometry model to drift out of step with the first. A terminal client can report its screen because its chrome is cell-shaped; a client whose chrome is PER PANE cannot, and this is what it reports instead.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/tiling.rs: the search is a walk DOWN from a bound, not a halving, and the reason is a property of `tile` worth stating: a window too small for both children of a split does not shrink them, it DROPS one and gives its region to the survivor — which then holds MORE cells than it did at the larger window. So "every pane fits" is not downward-closed; it is true at the answer, false just below it, and true again at the bottom. The bound is the fold of the measurements themselves, and nothing above it can fit, since the panes and dividers partition the window exactly.

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `retile(registry, attachments, session)` — every tiled pane resized to `tile(tree, window)`'s share, with a no-op guard on its current grid. THE move of the round: a pane's size is a function of two facts only the daemon holds, so a client computing it is re-deriving, and two re-derivations is exactly the defect this front keeps finding. `cell_px` is `(0, 0)` — a cell's pixel size is a property of a client's FONT, so the daemon does not invent one and does not have to, because the client that last set it still owns it.

crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the re-derivation runs at the mux action BOUNDARY (`invoke` splits into `dispatch` + the retile), not inside each action. Every action can move the arrangement, and one some actions performed and others forgot is R237's asymmetry; one site cannot forget. After the action's own work returns, so no pool lock is held across it.

crates/sprag-host/src/rpc.rs: `window_moved(state, session)` — the three ways a window moves without the tree changing (a client REPORTED, one ATTACHED, one DETACHED), each re-deriving BEFORE the bump, so a client woken by it reads a scene whose panes are already the size the new window gives them. `handle_attach`'s attachments guard is now bound and released first: written into a `match` scrutinee it lives for the whole match, and the arm re-reads that map.

crates/sprag-gui/src/reflow.rs: one client-wide Effect folds every tiled pane's measured rect (pinion's R1012 publish, which is the grid area with the header, scrollbar, divider and rounding already taken out by pinion's own layout) through `fit_window` and reports it. The per-pane pixel resize survives for exactly two cases, both of them "the session said nothing": a FLOATING pane (no leaf, so no tiling names it) and a host with no arbitrated window.

crates/sprag-tui/src/bin/sprag-tui.rs: the same sentence, one layer up — the terminal client keeps `tile` for PAINT and writes a pane's size only when `window_size()` is `None`. crates/sprag-terminal/src/layout.rs: `LayoutWire::panes()`, the tiled set as the tree's own shape rather than a client's pane list filtered by a floating flag.

crates/sprag-gui/src/bin/sprag-smoke.rs: `Smoke::attach_terminal` spawns a real `sprag-tui` on a real pseudoterminal through sprag's own `PanePty`, so the harness that had one frontend now has both. Dropping the handle is the detach. Grids are found by SHAPE (`sprag_gui.pane.*#grid`) rather than by slot number, because a slot is a display position earlier checks move panes in and out of.
verification_bullets: THE DEFECT WAS MEASURED BEFORE THE DESIGN WAS WRITTEN, and the numbers are what shaped it. The GUI need not model its chrome, because pinion already MEASURES each pane's laid-out rect; what it needs is the INVERSE of the tiler, folding those measurements back into one window. publishable_changes_bullets: crates/sprag-terminal/src/tiling.rs: `fit_window(tree, measured)` — the largest window whose tiling gives every pane no more cells than that pane's surface measured. It is the INVERSE of `tile` and is defined BY it: the search asks `tile` whether a candidate fits rather than doing arithmetic of its own, so there is no second geometry model to drift out of step with the first. A terminal client can report its screen because its chrome is cell-shaped; a client whose chrome is PER PANE cannot, and this is what it reports instead.

crates/sprag-terminal/src/tiling.rs: the search is a walk DOWN from a bound, not a halving, and the reason is a property of `tile` worth stating: a window too small for both children of a split does not shrink them, it DROPS one and gives its region to the survivor — which then holds MORE cells than it did at the larger window. So "every pane fits" is not downward-closed; it is true at the answer, false just below it, and true again at the bottom. The bound is the fold of the measurements themselves, and nothing above it can fit, since the panes and dividers partition the window exactly.

crates/sprag-host/src/window.rs: `retile(registry, attachments, session)` — every tiled pane resized to `tile(tree, window)`'s share, with a no-op guard on its current grid. crates/sprag-host/src/workspace.rs: the re-derivation runs at the mux action BOUNDARY (`invoke` splits into `dispatch` + the retile), not inside each action. Every action can move the arrangement, and one some actions performed and others forgot is R237's asymmetry; one site cannot forget.
